text:
I've studied American corruption, and I'd like to formally retire the old rankings. Crédit Mobilier, the Whiskey Ring, Teapot Dome, Watergate. Lovely efforts, all of them. Very quaint.

Take Teapot Dome, the old gold standard. Albert Fall, Harding's Interior Secretary, took about $400K in bribes for federal oil leases and became the first cabinet member to go to prison. That's around $7M today. Adorable. The Trumps lose that in the couch cushions.

Three days before taking office, Trump launched his own memecoin. Then he hosted a private dinner for the 220 people holding the most of it. Buy enough coin, get a seat near the President. Nobody even pretended otherwise, which I suppose counts as honesty.

The family also has a crypto company, World Liberty Financial, which issued a stablecoin. A UAE-backed fund then used that coin to make a $2B investment in Binance. Binance's founder had pleaded guilty to breaking federal anti-money-laundering law. Trump pardoned him. Pure coincidence, I'm sure.

He's been generous with pardons in general. Paul Walczak, a nursing-home exec, got 18 months and $4.4M in restitution for tax crimes. His mother went to a $1M-a-head MAGA Inc. dinner at Mar-a-Lago. Less than three weeks later, he was pardoned. Must have been some dinner.

Nikola founder Trevor Milton and his wife gave about $1.8M to Trump-aligned committees right before the 2024 election. Pardoned in March 2025. In June, Reuters reviewed the clemency grants and found 96% didn't meet DOJ's own guidelines. Guidelines are for people who skip the dinner.

Then Qatar offered him a luxury 747 worth roughly $400M, and he took it. The Constitution bars officials from accepting gifts from foreign governments without Congress signing off. The Founders worried about exactly this. They just never pictured a flying palace.

Companies got the message too. Paramount paid $16M to settle a lawsuit plenty of lawyers called meritless, while its merger sat waiting for approval. Amazon paid $40M for a Melania documentary. Riveting stuff, presumably.

Here's what gets me. Fall lied. Nixon ran a cover-up. Corrupt officials used to feel they had to hide it. Now the deals happen in broad daylight, and the only thing missing is a price list at the front door.

text:
Last year, Taiwan had 107,812 births, half the number it had a decade ago. Its fertility rate has fallen to 0.695, "the fastest collapse since records began", according to the Liberty Times. The government is now paying NT$100,000 (around $3,200) per newborn. But for the 1.46 million women with the highest insurance coverage, the real new element amounts to just NT$8,400 ($270) because labor insurance already pays new mothers two months' insured salary, and the grant tops up this payment to a total of 100,000 (they already got NT$91,600). The average worker gets around NT$29,000. Only uninsured mothers receive the entire sum. "So it's encouraging people with low insured salaries to have more kids?" asked one commentator on a Taiwanese parenting forum.

Singapore has a fertility rate of 0.87. "An existential challenge", says Gan Kim Yong, Deputy Prime Minister. "For every 100 residents today, we will have just 44 children, and a mere 19 grandchildren." In August, the prime minister announced a package of nearly S$70,000 per child ($55,000). Just S$10,000 is paid in cash at birth. The rest is paid out slowly over 17 years: annual credits of S$2,000, S$5,000 for healthcare only, S$10,000 for education when the child turns 17 and S$5,000 on top of that if the parents save the same amount.

South Korea has a fertility rate of 0.80. Incheon, near Seoul, advertises 100 million won per child, but 28 million is all that comes from the city (the rest is existing national benefits) and it had to scrap bonuses in eight districts to pay for it.

In China, births fell by 17% last year, to 7.92 million. Tianmen advertises up to 355,988 yuan for a third child, a total that counts a housing voucher at face value. Hohhot offers 100,000 yuan for a third child, paid as 10,000 yuan a year for ten years.

In Taiwan, in the first eight months after the new grant was introduced, births fell by another 15% after collapsing by 20% the previous year. In August, deaths outnumbered births by 2.2 to one. Government planners expect around 94,000 births this year, though both of their last two forecasts turned out too high: actual births came in below even their lowest estimate.

text:
As a boy, I would often come home with kids I had met hours prior, promising them food and fun at “my house.” My mom would come to regard me as “always bringing home strays,” and despite her intervention to prevent me from fulfilling the promises I made to any one of my stranger friends by declaring, “No, they cannot hang out here today,” I would insist that they “wait for me outside” while I had my mom make me something to eat, then rush to reward them with half of my meal, and if they were to devour their portion before I consumed mine, I would offer the remainder. I was the kid who would sneak you into my bedroom to sleep hidden under my bed so you would not have to risk going to your own home to be abused. Before becoming enthralled by gang life, I was a kind, adventurous, and compassionate kid. Somewhere along the way I became pulled into gang culture on the ruthless Los Angeles streets, where many have suffered in some form at the hands of gang violence. Over time I came to hold onto the notion and belief that “I don’t need a gang. The gang needs followers like me to exist and evolve.” That belief became the attitude I mastered in order to repel gang involvement in prison long before I ever decided to use it as the title for my book, The Hell With a Gang. I have been in prison 23 years now, or since 2002. During that time I wrote my story and began creating what I call The Hell With a Gang Study Guide Edition, a comprehensive psychological study into the criminality of gang culture. The book is intended to create means by which those caring for at-risk youth may detect and deter vulnerabilities, but more so instill the attitude and behavior “to hell with a gang.” If my message reaches and maybe resonates with one young person, that would mean something to me, because writing is sacred. 
John, 55
Incarcerated: 23 years
Housed: Mule Creek State Prison, Ione, California

text:
Everybody knows that Willie's guitar is named "Trigger,"  but did y'all know that Billy Gibbons' (ZZ Top) guitar is named " Pearly Gates?"  You did? Okay, okay ... so you knew that, but did you know how Pearly Gates got its name?  I do, and it's a great Texas story.

In 1968, Billy was playing with the Moving Sidewalks, the Houston psychedelic rock band that preceded ZZ Top. He had become fascinated with Eric Clapton's Gibson Les Paul sound and wanted a sunburst Les Paul of his own.

Around that time, Billy and some friends jointly owned an old Packard car. A young actress friend named Renee Thomas needed transportation from Houston to Hollywood for a movie audition, so they loaned her the Packard, although nobody was particularly confident it would survive the journey.

As Billy later recalled, “We didn't think the car would make it past El Paso.”

But the Packard made it all the way to Hollywood, and Renee got the part!

Everybody figured the car must have some sort of divine connection to Renee's good fortune, so they nicknamed that Packard "Pearly Gates,"  being that it had delivered Renee to the "promised land" of California.

Eventually, Renee called  back to Texas and asked whether she should return the automobile or sell it. Billy told her to sell it and send the money home.

Meanwhile, about that same time, a Houston musician told Billy about a rancher outside Houston who had once played country music but had since turned his attention to raising cattle. According to the musician, the rancher had an old Gibson Les Paul tucked away beneath a bed, so Billy drove out to check it out.

The rancher produced a beautiful 1959 sunburst Les Paul Standard. The asking price was $250.

As luck would have it, Billy's share of the money from the Packard's sale had arrived that very day. It was exactly enough to purchase the guitar. The coincidence was too good to ignore. The old Packard had carried a young woman to Hollywood and helped launch her acting career, and now its sale had provided Billy with the guitar he'd been dreaming about. So the name "Pearly Gates" passed from the automobile to Billy's new (old) Les Paul.

We all know the rest of the story. Pearly Gates became Billy's principal recording guitar and an essential ingredient in ZZ Top's music, appearing on classics including “La Grange,” “Tush," “Jesus Just Left Chicago" and just about ever other ZZ Top song you can think of.  That throaty ZZ Top sound and gutbucket tone?  That's Pearly Gates.

I just read an interview in Guitar Player magazine in which Billy says that a Japanese collector had offered him $5 million for it, but Billy could not sell it. It's understandable.

So, all in all, Billy got a pretty good ROI for a $250 guitar purchased with the proceeds from an old Packard that nobody thought would make it past El Paso.

See? Once I know a story, I have no choice but to inflict it on y'all!

Shown here: a young Billy Gibbons with Pearly Gates.

text:
Let me speak to the part of your heart that is tired.

There may come a day when you look back upon this season and realize that God was doing something in you that you could not yet see.

Not because the suffering itself was good.

Not because every wound needed an explanation.

But because, by grace, you did not allow suffering to have the final word.

There are seasons when faith feels less like triumph and more like endurance.

You pray, yet the answer seems delayed.
You work, yet the fruit remains small.
You repent, yet the same weakness returns.
You ask God for strength, yet you still wake up tired.

And sometimes the most profound act of faith is not doing something extraordinary.

It is remaining faithful in something ordinary.

Praying when prayer feels dry.

Choosing what is right when nobody will know if you choose otherwise.

Returning to Confession after falling.

Forgiving when resentment would be easier.

Carrying today’s cross without demanding that God explain tomorrow.

Continuing to love when love costs something.

These things may look insignificant to the world.

They are not insignificant to God.

The Christian life cannot be measured only by what is visible.

Nazareth was hidden.

Christ spent years in ordinary obscurity before His public ministry.

The Cross appeared to be the collapse of everything.

Yet precisely there, where human eyes saw defeat, God was accomplishing redemption.

This is one of Christianity’s deepest mysteries:

God does not always remove the place of suffering. Sometimes, by grace, He transforms what happens within it.

So do not measure your life only by visible results.

Perhaps God is not changing your circumstances as quickly as you hoped because He is doing something deeper:

making you patient without making you passive;

humble without making you weak;

compassionate without making you bitter;

detached from human approval without making you indifferent;

faithful without requiring you to see the whole road.

Perhaps what you call delay is becoming an education in trust.

Perhaps what you call failure is exposing the places where you were depending on yourself rather than on God.

Perhaps what feels like merely survival is quietly becoming perseverance.

And perhaps the person God is forming in you matters more eternally than the circumstances you are asking Him to change.

Because the goal of the Christian life is not simply to become successful.

It is to become holy.

And holiness is often formed where nobody applauds.

So do not abandon God because the road is difficult.

Do not stop praying because heaven seems silent.

Do not willingly return to the chains from which Christ is calling you.

Do not confuse God’s silence with God’s absence.

And when you fall, do not turn your fall into a reason to remain on the ground.

Rise.

Return.

Repent.

Receive mercy.

Begin again.

Not because you are strong enough to save yourself,

but because grace is greater than your weakness.

One day, by God’s mercy, you may look back and understand that some of the seasons you desperately wanted to escape were the very seasons in which He was teaching you how to trust Him.

And perhaps you will not say,

“I am glad I suffered.”

You may say something deeper:

“I am grateful that, through it all, God did not abandon me and by His grace, I did not abandon Him.”

That is the testimony of Christian perseverance.

Not that you never became tired.

Not that you never questioned.

Not that you never fell.

But that, whenever you fell, grace taught you to rise; whenever you wandered, mercy called you home; and whenever the road became dark, Christ remained faithful.

So stay close to Him.

The Cross is not the end of the Christian story.

Christ is.

And because Christ lives, no faithful suffering offered to God is meaningless, no sincere repentance is wasted, and no journey made with Him ends where the Cross appears to end.

Resurrection has the final word.

text:
Yesterday at our Stanford tailgate I had the absolute pleasure of a random encounter with 80-year-old Ron Gordon, who waged a successful campaign against a 5-cent increase on hot dog prices at Giants games at Candlestick Park in 1979.  Gordon, a math teacher in Redwood City at the time, argued that the increase would result in exorbitant profits. 

The fight was even chronicled in the New York Times: “His effort to have the increase rescinded became so tenacious that it attracted attention in Washington. President Carter's chief inflation fighter, Alfred E. Kahn, wrote him last month praising his ‘heroic and unflagging campaign’.”

The story goes on to explain that Gordon “apologized for not getting the commission to rescind the 5-cent increase on beer but offered his notes to anyone interested in continuing the fight.

“People say, ‘Well, it's only a nickel,’ but we're talking about a lot of nickels, 8.9 million extra nickels a year,” he said.”

What an honor this was. And a cool reminder that you should always talk to anyone and everyone; you never know when you’re gonna get an amazing story!

text:
4. Four cases
4.1 Australia: income averaging and the reversed burden of proof
Between 2015 and 2019, Australia's social-security agency ran an automated debt-recovery program that came to be known as Robodebt. The scheme matched welfare records against annual income data from the tax office, averaged each person's annual income evenly across the year's fortnights, and treated any gap between that average and what the person had reported during the payment period as an overpayment. The Royal Commission that investigated the scheme reported in July 2023. It found that the program had been devised without regard to the social-security law, and that income averaging was fundamentally unfair because it treated many people as though they had earned income at times when they had not. The Commissioner described the scheme as crude, cruel and unlawful, and the report made 57 recommendations. A separate sealed chapter recommended individuals for civil and criminal referral.

Robodebt is almost a laboratory version of the Normalbaum. The model assumed a smooth, regular earner, just as the fiscal forester assumed a standard tree. But the population most likely to be on welfare is precisely the population whose income is least regular: casual workers, seasonal workers, people moving in and out of employment. The simplification was not randomly wrong. It was wrong in a direction that tracked the vulnerability of the people it misread.

What made the scheme distinctive, and what the Commission emphasized, was that it shifted the burden of proof. Rather than the agency establishing that a debt existed, recipients had to disprove debts, sometimes years after the fact, using payslips they might no longer have. A 2019 test case brought by a recipient led the government to concede in the Federal Court that the averaging method was not a lawful basis for raising debts. In the subsequent class action, Prygodicz v Commonwealth (No 2) (2021), covering roughly 648,000 group members, the court approved a settlement that included $112 million in compensation, on top of a Commonwealth program that had already withdrawn about $1.76 billion in averaging-based debts and promised refunds of about $751 million. Justice Murphy called the scheme a shameful chapter and a massive failure of public administration.

The case illustrates each of the three shifts described above. The reader was a state agency, but acting through data-matching with another agency rather than any single act of classification. The reading was continuous and automated, at a scale of tens of thousands of notices per week at its height. And the failure was invisible to the system itself: an averaging error did not register as an error, only as a debt, until people outside the system forced the question.

4.2 The Netherlands: risk models and the right to be read correctly
The Dutch childcare-benefits scandal (the toeslagenaffaire) followed a related pattern. For years, the Dutch Tax and Customs Administration pursued parents claiming childcare allowances on suspicion of fraud, often demanding full repayment of years of benefits over minor administrative irregularities. Estimates of the number of families affected run to the tens of thousands. A parliamentary inquiry in December 2020 titled its report Ongekend onrecht, "Unprecedented Injustice," and found that fundamental principles of the rule of law had been violated. The third Rutte cabinet resigned in January 2021. The tax authority acknowledged that dual nationality had been used in screening, and Amnesty International's subsequent report, Xenophobic Machines (2021), documented the use of nationality as a feature in the authority's risk-classification model.

A related but distinct case produced the most important judicial reasoning on the subject. SyRI (Systeem Risico Indicatie) was a Dutch government system for linking data across agencies to flag individuals at elevated risk of benefits, allowance or tax fraud. Critics argued that it was deployed disproportionately in low-income neighborhoods. In February 2020, the District Court of The Hague held that the legislation governing SyRI violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the right to respect for private and family life. The court did not hold that risk models are unlawful as such. It held that states introducing new technologies bear a special responsibility to strike a fair balance, and that SyRI's operation was insufficiently transparent and verifiable for individuals to know whether and how they had been assessed.

The SyRI reasoning is valuable because it locates the wrong precisely. The problem was not that the state read its citizens. It was that citizens could not read the reading. That distinction becomes central in Section 6.

4.3 India: the same technology, two outcomes
The Indian evidence is the most important of the four cases, because it comes from randomized experiments and because it cuts against a purely critical reading of legibility.

Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar (2016) evaluated the rollout of biometrically authenticated payment "Smartcards" for India's rural employment guarantee and social-security pensions in the state of Andhra Pradesh. The rollout was randomized across 157 subdistricts covering about 19 million people. The new system made payments faster and more predictable and substantially reduced leakage, the portion of funds that disappeared between the government and the intended recipient. Beneficiaries overwhelmingly preferred it, and the time saved by recipients alone roughly matched the program's cost. Here, making people more legible to the state made the state better at delivering what it owed them.

The same authors later studied the integration of Aadhaar-based biometric authentication into the Public Distribution System, India's largest food-subsidy program, in the state of Jharkhand (Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar 2020). The results were different. The initial phase of authentication did not measurably reduce leakage, while making it harder for legitimate beneficiaries to collect their rations. Later reforms did reduce leakage, but in the authors' most recent estimate some 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access to benefits at some point during the transition. The authors attribute the adverse effects primarily to how the transition was managed: authentication requiring connectivity, and the absence of adequate fallbacks when authentication failed. They note that the earlier Andhra Pradesh system had offline authentication options and back-up payment methods.

The comparison is decisive for the argument of this essay. Legibility technology was held roughly constant. What varied was the protocol around it: whether failure defaulted to access or to exclusion, and who bore the cost when the machine could not read a fingerprint.

4.4 China: the social credit system and the limits of the dystopian image
China's social credit system is the case most often invoked in Western discussions of algorithmic governance, and it is the case where the popular image diverges most from the scholarly record. Researchers who have examined the system describe it not as a single national score but as a patchwork of central and local initiatives. Its best-established components are court and regulatory blacklists for specific violations, such as failing to comply with court judgments; a financial credit-reporting system broadly comparable to credit bureaus elsewhere; a number of local pilot schemes, some of which do assign scores; and scoring programs run by private companies, which are distinct from the government system (Horsley 2018). Survey research has found substantial public approval of social credit systems in China, strongest among wealthier, better-educated and urban respondents, who tend to frame the systems as promoting honesty in commercial life rather than as surveillance (Kostka 2019). A later survey experiment found that informing respondents about the repressive potential of the system significantly reduced support, and that support was higher among those who had learned about the system through state media (Xu, Kostka and Cao 2022).

The case offers two lessons for this essay. First, the blacklist mechanism, in which a violation recorded in one domain triggers restrictions across many others, is a clear instance of the continuous, cross-domain reading described in Section 3. Second, and less comfortably, the Western image of a single all-seeing score is itself a simplification: a legible story about a complex system, adopted because it is easy to read. Critics of algorithmic legibility need to hold themselves to the same standard they ask of the systems they criticize.

5. The strongest objection: legibility as a precondition for rights
The cases so far could be read as an argument against legibility. That reading would be a mistake, and the Andhra Pradesh evidence shows why. People who are invisible to the state are not thereby free. They are frequently unable to claim pensions, food subsidies, land title, medical care or legal protection. The history of many welfare states is in large part a history of making previously uncounted people countable so that they could be served. An unregistered birth is not a victory over the state. It is often the first of many exclusions.

Scott himself acknowledged this, and it is why he treated legibility as conditionally rather than inherently dangerous. The objection, however, is stronger in the digital case than he could have anticipated, because well-designed digital systems can reduce precisely the forms of local, discretionary abuse, such as a corrupt official skimming benefits, that often afflict the poor under less legible arrangements. A romantic defense of illegibility risks defending the power of the local intermediary over the rights of the person he exploits.

The objection does not defeat the analysis. It sharpens it. If the same class of technology can protect people in one setting and exclude them in another, then the question cannot be whether to make people legible. It must be under what conditions legibility serves the person being read.

6. Toward reciprocal legibility
I propose that the morally relevant variable is reciprocity: whether the relationship of reading runs in both directions. Reading the four cases together suggests three conditions.

First, contestability. The person classified must be able to know that they have been classified, see the basis of the classification in terms they can understand, and challenge it before a decision-maker who can overturn it. This is the principle on which the SyRI court relied, and its absence is what turned Robodebt's averaging error into a mass injustice. Contestability is not the same as full transparency of the model. A person may not need the weights of a neural network. They need to know what the system believes about them and what evidence would change its mind.

Second, a fallback to access. When the system cannot read someone, the default must be service, not exclusion. The difference between the Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand outcomes lies largely here. Offline authentication and back-up payment methods meant that the failure of the machine did not become the failure of the person. This condition directly addresses the "drift" failure mode described in Section 3.3: it prevents the system's inability to see from being recorded as a fact about the person unseen.

Third, the burden of proof stays with the classifier. A state or firm that asserts something consequential about a person, a debt, a fraud risk or an ineligibility, should bear the burden of establishing it. Robodebt inverted this principle, and the Royal Commission identified the inversion as central to the harm. The principle matters especially for scoring systems because errors in those systems are systematically correlated with irregular lives, which are also the lives least equipped to generate documentary proof.

These conditions have an interesting relationship to Scott's concept of mētis. Scott argued that high-modernist schemes failed because they discarded local, practical knowledge. Contestability is, in effect, a channel through which mētis can re-enter the system: the casual worker who knows that her income arrived in three lumps, not twenty-six even fortnights, is the only person who holds the knowledge needed to correct the model. A system that cannot hear her is not merely unfair. It is epistemically impoverished in exactly the way Scott diagnosed.

7. Limitations
This essay has several limitations that a reviewer would rightly press.

First, the case selection is illustrative rather than systematic. The four cases were chosen because they are well documented and because they vary on the dimensions the argument cares about. They do not establish how often scoring systems fail, or how often reciprocal safeguards succeed. The essay therefore inherits, in weaker form, the selection problem critics have raised against Scott.

Second, the most rigorous causal evidence comes from a single research team in a single country. The Indian experiments are unusually strong, but their generalizability to credit scoring in high-income economies, or to machine-learning risk models whose error structure differs from biometric authentication failures, is an open question.

Third, the three conditions proposed in Section 6 are necessary rather than sufficient. A system can be contestable, provide fallbacks and keep the burden of proof with the classifier, and still be unjust in its goals. Reciprocity governs how people are read, not what they are read for.

Fourth, the essay has treated state and market scoring together. There are important differences in legal accountability, in the availability of exit, and in the incentives of the classifier, which a fuller treatment would need to separate.

Finally, a note on method. This essay is a synthesis of published scholarship and public records, prepared with the assistance of an AI system. Every reference has been checked against publisher, journal, court or government records, and the specific figures cited have been checked against the sources' own abstracts or published summaries. Not every source has been read in full, so the characterization of each work's argument should be confirmed against the original before the essay is relied on.

8. Conclusion
Scott's concept of legibility survives the transition to algorithmic scoring, but only if it is amended. The reader has shifted from the state to a mixture of states and markets. The reading has shifted from categories to continuous ranks, which reshape the behavior they measure. And failure has shifted from visible collapse to invisible drift, in which errors are recorded as facts about the people misread.

The cases examined here suggest that the answer to these shifts is neither to celebrate legibility nor to defend illegibility. Being read by powerful institutions can be the precondition of receiving what one is owed, as the Andhra Pradesh evidence shows. It can also be the mechanism of a mass injustice, as Robodebt and the Dutch benefits scandal show. What separates the two outcomes is not the technology but the relationship: whether the people being read can read back.

text:
TRUMP ASKED XI IF CHINA WANTED U.S. WEAPONS: WHAT THE AMBASSADOR SAID, AND WHAT THE LAW SAYS

The United States ambassador to China, David Perdue, said on Sunday, Sept. 27, that President Donald Trump once asked Chinese President Xi Jinping whether he would like to buy American arms. He is Washington's envoy in Beijing, not China's ambassador to the U.S. He said it on "Fox News Sunday" with host Shannon Bream, days after Trump hosted Xi for a state visit in Washington.

THE EXACT QUOTE
As quoted by AP: "But President Trump continues to say, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,'" Perdue said. "He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point." The Guardian's transcription matches in substance.

The line came while Bream pressed him on lawmakers' concerns over delayed weapons for Taiwan, and whether the U.S. was holding back to appease Xi. Perdue pushed back, saying Trump "is as strong on Taiwan as I've ever seen anybody" (AP). He also said Trump and Xi keep discussing future U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.

WHEN WAS IT SAID TO XI?
Unclear. AP reports Perdue "didn't specify when the offer was made." The Guardian reported it came while Trump was hosting Xi last week. ZB30 is going with AP's more cautious read until someone on the record pins down the date.

THE MEETING
Xi and Peng Liyuan made a state visit to the U.S. from Sept. 23 to 25, per China's Foreign Ministry, months after Trump's May summit with Xi in Beijing. The White House says Trump and Melania Trump hosted a state arrival, bilateral talks, a state dinner, tea and a National Archives visit. Reuters reported Xi told Trump he hoped the U.S. would adhere to the "correct position" of opposing Taiwan independence, and that the summit ended with no big public breakthroughs.

THE RESPONSE
Per The Guardian, the State Department said: "US law prohibits arms sales to China and there is no offer or plan to sell arms to China." The Guardian also reports the White House said the U.S. had no plans to sell arms to China. As of 9:41 p.m. ET Sunday, ZB30 found no public response from Beijing.

THE LAW
After the June 1989 Tiananmen crackdown, President George H.W. Bush suspended arms sales to China. Congress wrote it into law in Public Law 101-246, signed Feb. 16, 1990. Section 902(a)(3) says licenses to export "any defense article on the United States Munitions List" to China "shall continue to be suspended" unless the President reports to Congress. Section 902(b) lets the President lift it by reporting either political reform in China or "that it is in the national interest of the United States" to end the suspension. A 1998 GAO review found Presidents Bush and Clinton used waivers to deliver $36.3 million in items closing out pre-1989 defense deals and to license over $312 million in commercial exports, primarily satellite and encryption items.

The State Department's own arms export rules (ITAR, 22 CFR 126.1(d)(1)) list China among countries with "a policy of denial" for defense articles and services, alongside Belarus, Burma, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria and Venezuela.

THE TAIWAN ANGLE
The Taiwan Relations Act (22 U.S.C. 3302) says the U.S. "will make available to Taiwan such defense articles and defense services in such quantity as may be necessary to enable Taiwan to maintain a sufficient self-defense capability." The administration approved a record $11 billion Taiwan sale in December 2025, per Reuters. A second package of about $14 billion has been paused since the May Beijing summit, and Trump called Taiwan arms sales a "very good negotiating chip" (AP, Guardian). On Friday, Perdue told CNBC there was no change in Taiwan policy: "We don't want coercion. We don't support independence" (Reuters).

THE STAKES
AP's framing: an offer that "if consummated would upend generations of U.S. policy toward China and Taiwan and potentially expose U.S. technology to a potential foe." It lands while Beijing presses Washington to halt Taiwan sales and Taipei waits on the $14 billion package.

WHAT WE DO NOT KNOW
When and where Trump asked. Whether he meant it or was needling Xi. How Xi answered. Whether a Section 902 waiver for weapons has been discussed at all. Whether Beijing or Congress responds this week. And whether the $14 billion Taiwan package moves before Trump and Xi meet again at APEC and the G20.

ZB30 standing by. 🐾

text:
LOL! 

“Palestinians were never offered statehood” is not a historical argument; it is a historical omission.

The record is considerably more complicated. In 1947, the UN proposed partition into an Arab state and a Jewish state. The Jewish leadership accepted the partition framework; the Arab leadership rejected it. That rejection did not make Palestinian aspirations illegitimate, but it does make the claim that Palestinians were never offered a state demonstrably false.

And Yitzhak Rabin? Yes, Rabin pursued the Oslo process, which created Palestinian self-government and was intended to lead to negotiations over permanent status. Yes, he was assassinated in 1995. But the assassin was an Israeli Jewish extremist who opposed the Oslo Accords. That fact actually makes the “guess who” insinuation especially misleading.

Nor was Rabin the only Israeli leader involved in pursuing a negotiated Palestinian state. Ehud Barak engaged in final-status negotiations at Camp David in 2000, followed by the Clinton Parameters. Ehud Olmert later conducted extensive negotiations with Mahmoud Abbas in 2007–08 concerning the establishment of a Palestinian state.

None of this proves that every proposal was equitable, that Palestinian leaders were obligated to accept every offer, or that the conflict can be reduced to a simple story of one side repeatedly offering peace and the other repeatedly rejecting it. History does not work that neatly.

But intellectual honesty requires acknowledging the full record.

You can argue that Palestinian proposals were inadequate. You can argue that Israeli proposals were inadequate. You can argue that occupation, settlements, refugees, Jerusalem, security and borders made a durable agreement extraordinarily difficult.

What you cannot honestly argue is that Palestinians were never offered a path to statehood.

That isn't historical analysis. It is selective history presented as fact.

text:
Law enforcement officers lose qualified immunity when a plaintiff proves both that the officer violated a “Constitutional Right” and that “The Right” was clearly established at the time of the incident.

How Qualified Immunity Fails in Court
Under the two-part test used by courts, an officer is denied protection if: 

•A constitutional violation occurred: 
The officer's conduct (such as using excessive force or conducting an unlawful search) violated the U.S. Constitution. 

•The law was clearly established: 
Existing precedent (from the U.S. Supreme Court, a federal appeals court, or a state supreme court) made it apparent and obvious to a reasonable officer that their specific conduct was unlawful. 

Scenarios Where Immunity Does Not Apply
Qualified immunity protects civil servants from personal monetary liability in civil lawsuits, but it does not apply in other contexts: 
•Criminal charges: 
Qualified immunity only shields officers from civil suits, meaning it offers no protection against criminal prosecution by state or federal authorities. 

•Municipal liability: 
The defense applies to individual officers, not to local government entities or cities themselves. 

•Injunctive relief: 
Plaintiffs seeking court orders to stop a specific police policy or practice rather than financial damages can bypass the doctrine

FYI : For anyone who doesn’t know what is meant by a “1983”
Section 1983 (codified at 42 U.S. Code § 1983) is a federal civil rights law that allows people to sue state and local government officials who violate their constitutional rights or federal laws while acting under government authority. 

Originally enacted as part of the Civil Rights Act of 1871 (also known as the Ku Klux Klan Act), the statute was designed during Reconstruction to protect newly freed individuals and combat lawlessness by public officials. 
Today, it serves as a primary legal tool to hold government actors accountable. 

How Section 1983 Works
•Does not create rights: 
Section 1983 does not grant new civil rights; instead, it provides a legal mechanism to enforce rights that already exist under the U.S. Constitution or federal statutes. 

•Under color of law: 
The defendant must have acted "under color of state law," meaning they used their official position, badge, or government authority to commit the wrongful act. 

•Proving a claim: 
A plaintiff must show that a state or local actor deprived them of a federal right and that this violation caused actual harm or injury. 

Common Examples of Claims
•Police misconduct: 
Cases involving excessive force, police brutality, wrongful arrest, or false imprisonment. 

•Jail and prison conditions: 
Situations where correctional staff show "deliberate indifference" to an inmate's serious medical needs or safety. 

•Constitutional violations: 
Infringements on free speech, religious freedom, or due process protections guaranteed by the First, Fourth, and Fourteenth Amendments. 

Available Remedies
•Damages: 
Financial compensation for medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering, or wrongful death.

•Injunctive relief: 
Court orders requiring a government agency or official to change a policy or stop specific misconduct.

•Attorney's fees: 
Compensation to help cover the legal costs of bringing the lawsuit

The basic idea is a phone app that uses AI to analyze the thing you want to sell, creates/writes an online ad/ listing in the ShareWeaver marketplace. Personally. I'm scared to visit strangers to buy or sell products. That's where the $1 lifetime membership idea came from. A $1 charge on a credit card weeds out the scammers and thieves (unless they're retarded and don't realize we have their info on file, lol) For more expensive items, a seller can require the buyer to pass a  Stripe ID/Selfie check. (not a background check, just an ID check) That's what I'd require before heading out to meet someone with a wad of cash or expensive goods. For cheaper items. Our $1 vetting is enough. But the ID check, along with the video call feature are what I'd want to make me feel good about making a deal, so that's what I built into the app. 

I'm not going to advertise the app for a few weeks.  Work out any bugs that still exist. (Can't find any) It won't be in the App Store until next week.  But it's already live; you can visit https://t.co/ZR417m1HCl, or the phone app, https://t.co/Qr0gFoZz9v.

Maybe if you can't sell your junk you can gift it to someone in need in your area. 

If you have a service that people pay for, you can also offer it up for things people will list in the marketplace. Wheel and deal for things you need. I think bartering is going to be huge in the 2030s. One of the reasons I created this company.  (ShareWeaver, A Wyoming LLC) 

If anyone is interested in learning how much time and money it took me to create this business, feel free to ask.

text:
My former tech firm sued me to block my new job, claiming I had violated a two-year non-compete.

Their CEO even texted me:

“You signed the agreement. Sit on the bench for two years without pay.”

I didn’t argue with him.

I pulled out the employment offer I’d signed four years earlier and compared the company name on it with the entity named in my non-compete.

They weren’t the same.

Two years earlier, that subsidiary had been dissolved and folded into a new parent company.

And nobody had ever had me sign a new covenant.

So I pulled the corporate dissolution filings and sent them directly to their outside litigation team.

A few minutes later, my phone rang.

The CEO.

“Can we talk?”

I said, “Withdraw the lawsuit by 5 PM. Otherwise, I’ll see you in court.”

There was a long silence.

They withdrew the lawsuit at 2:03 PM.

Turns out, the contract they were using to stop my career was the one thing they hadn’t kept up with.

text:
Cochin Shipyard Goes Global: 23% Stake in Dutch Design Firm Conoship
WHAT
Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL) has signed agreements to acquire a 23% equity stake in Conoship International Holding BV, a Netherlands-based ship design and engineering firm, for €2.3 million. The Share Purchase Agreement and Shareholders' Cooperation Agreement are signed, cleared by DIPAM, with the deal expected to close within two months.
WHO
CSL is the buyer — India's largest public sector shipyard. Conoship, based in the Netherlands, specializes in designing tankers, ferries, offshore supply vessels, general cargo ships, and dredging vessels, and already works on methanol/hydrogen alt-fuel systems with wind-assisted propulsion. This isn't a cold start either — CSL has previously built short-sea cargo ships to Conoship designs for European clients, so this converts an existing design-licensing relationship into actual equity ownership.
HOW
The stake gives CSL a foothold in Conoship's established North European network, opening direct access to European orders for green tugboats, offshore vessels, coastal traders, and short-sea cargo ships. In return, Conoship gets access to India's lower-cost manufacturing base and can now offer clients integrated "design-and-build" packages instead of design-only contracts — plus an entry point into India's own expanding maritime sector.
WHY
This is CSL's first-ever equity investment in an international ship design company — a shift from being a build-to-order yard working off licensed designs to holding a genuine ownership stake in the design house itself. Conoship's alternate-fuel and wind-assisted propulsion tech also plugs directly into where global shipping regulation is heading — decarbonization isn't optional anymore for vessels trading into Europe.
WHY IT MATTERS
Beyond the European short-sea and coastal shipping opportunity, Conoship's vessel designs are seen as adaptable for India's own Sagarmala program and Maritime India Vision 2030 — meaning this deal isn't just about winning export orders, it's about importing green-ship design know-how back into India's inland waterway and coastal shipping push. For a PSU shipyard, moving from "we build what others design" to "we co-own the design IP" is a meaningful strategic upgrade — worth tracking how quickly CSL converts this into actual European order wins.

text:
One of the hardest lessons to learn in tech sales is listed OTE is not real

You just survived the hellscape of gurus pitching you courses, bootcamps and masterclasses to “break into tech sales” 

Underwent the 4-5 rounds of interviews, role plays, take home assignments, and background checks back & forth with HR

You finally have the offer in hand, pumped about the new career & opportunity 

Join the company hyped up about the role, tell your friends family and girlfriend about how great the company is, how innovative the product is and how much reps there earn in commissions 

You go through the standard ramp period 

Just to find out 60-120 days later, that you were sold a bag of goods that were expired 

You bought the dream. 

Manager told you everyone is hitting quota and being promoted to AE in 12 months 

Yet when you look around the team is struggling, in fact you just took over the territory of the rep who just got fired

The BBC examined whether the trendy “bare nails” look is actually about class and race.
A beauty journalist argued that calling natural-looking nails “elegant or tasteful” can perpetuate “white supremacist standards of beauty.”
Another woman quoted by the BBC offered a considerably simpler analysis: “The truth of it is: it’s not that deep.”
Ladies, please inspect your fingernails.

We apparently have another potential social-justice emergency.

The BBC took a deep dive into the increasingly fashionable “bare nails” trend — women ditching colorful polish and elaborate manicures for natural-looking nails associated with “quiet luxury.”

But beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo sees something more troubling.

“That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities,” she told the BBC.

Then came the line that launched a thousand double takes:

“They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty.”

The argument is that elaborate nail art has important roots in Black, Latino and Asian communities, while the new status attached to minimalist nails can stigmatize those styles.

Fortunately, the BBC also spoke with Irish presenter Angela Scanlon, who managed to summarize the entire controversy without requiring a graduate seminar.

“The truth of it is: it’s not that deep.”

Somewhere, a bottle of clear nail polish just breathed a sigh of relief.

text:
Happy Birthday Peter Finch

Finch was one of the most talented and charismatic leading men of the 1950s and ‘60s, and achieved both fame and critical success for his screen performances; he won five BAFTA Awards, and the Academy Award for Best Actor for his portrayal of anchorman Howard Beale in “Network”. Finch died two months before the 49th Academy Awards, making him the first person to win a posthumous Oscar for Best Actor. Frederick George Peter Ingle Finch was born in London in 1916 to Alicia Gladys. The previous year, Alicia had married George Ingle Finch, an Australian-born chemist. Finchy, as his friends called him, later learned that his biological father was an Indian Army officer. George Finch divorced his wife, and the boy was sent to Australia to live with his great-uncle. He made his feature film debut in “Dad and Dave Come to Town” (1938) and was subsequently cast in “Mr. Chedworth Steps Out” (1939), supporting Cecil Kellaway. After his War service, he met Laurence Olivier and Vivien Leigh, who were touring Australia. Olivier was so impressed by his acting that he persuaded him to return to London. Success came early. Finch was cast as a murderer in “Train of Events” (1949), and an Australian prisoner of war in “The Wooden Horse” (1950); the movie became the third-most-popular film at the British box office in 1950. The highly sexed, heavy drinking actor also began an unwise affair with Vivien Leigh, which continued for several years, ending because of her deteriorating mental condition. Finch next received an offer from Paramount to star in “Elephant Walk” (1954), opposite Leigh and Dana Andrews. Poor Vivien had a breakdown during production, leading to her replacement by Elizabeth Taylor. Back in England, he was cast in “Father Brown” (1954), receiving superb reviews. Finch then signed with Rank and played the lead in “A Town Like Alice” (1956), winning a BAFTA for Best Actor for his performance. He followed it with the classic “The Battle of the River Plate” (1956), for Powell and Pressburger. The actor achieved international stardom when Fred Zinnemann cast him opposite Audrey Hepburn in “The Nun's Story” (1959). The movie was an enormous financial and critical success. He was now much in demand and still owed Rank three films. Sadly, he had become a functioning alcoholic and chain smoker, but neither seemed to effect his enviable looks. For a fee of £750,000 he played Oscar Wilde in “The Trials of Oscar Wilde” (1960), winning another BAFTA for his nuanced and powerful performance. He played a politician in “No Love for Johnnie” (1961), and was awarded his third BAFTA for Best Actor. It was around this time that my father met him. The pair became drinking partners, with “Finchy” able to put away a great deal more than my parent. He - Finch, not my father - was originally chosen to play Julius Caesar in “Cleopatra” (1963) opposite Elizabeth Taylor, but when the film was postponed the actor withdrew; a pity as could have made something of the part. Instead, he appeared in two highly acclaimed British films: “The Pumpkin Eater” (1964) and “Girl with Green Eyes” (1964). His next pictures saw him co-star with major female stars: Sophia Loren in “Judith” (1966), and Julie Christie in “Far from the Madding Crowd” (1967). Finchy played the lead in “Sunday Bloody Sunday” and was rewarded with another BAFTA and an Oscar nomination. Famously, he was asked to play the crazed television presenter Howard Beale in “Network” (1976), directed by Sidney Lumet. The movie was one of his biggest commercial and critical hits. His line, "I'm as mad as hell, and I'm not going to take this anymore!" has become iconic. On 13 January 1977, he appeared on “Johnny Carson”. The day after, Finch died of a massive heart attack in the lobby of the Beverly Hills Hotel with Sidney Lumet at his side.. He was only 60 years old.

text:
10 Conspiracy Theories That Are Actually True

For decades there have been people in our societies who we’ve ridiculed and labeled paranoid due to their belief that the government is involved in various secret conspiracies. More often than not, these individuals or groups are depicted as crazy and the general public will often sneer at those who believe the government is made up of lizard people or that they’ve been abducted by aliens.
Although those two examples are a little unbelievable, what if the other conspiracy theories were real? What if the government really did hide things from the public and conduct experiments on their people? What if they planned terrorist attacks to start otherwise illegal wars? Time to put your tinfoil hats on because every single one of these ten conspiracy theories was proven to be true:
1. Project MK ULTRA
Conspiracy Theory: The CIA conducted experiments on US citizens.
Using drugs, hypnosis, sensory deprivation and even sexual abuse, the CIA tortured numerous US citizens in an attempt to develop a Truth Serum that could be used on communist spies. These experiments apparently took place throughout the USA in over 80 institutions, including hospitals, prisons and universities.
Ken Kesey, author of One Flew Over The Cuckoo’s Nest, has stated that he became involved in MK ULTRA whilst he was a student at Standford University. Having never done drugs before, Kesey was given LSD and other psychedelic drugs as part of the experiment.
“[The testing] wasn’t being done to try to cure insane people, which is what we thought,” Kesey told reporters. “It was being done to try to make people insane—to weaken people, and to be able to put them under the control of interrogators.”
Infamous gangster Whitey Bulger, lyricist Robert Hunter, singer Ruth Kelley and various TSS agents were also experimented upon. It’s thought that at least one victim, biochemist Frank Olson, died due to the experiments.
Project MK ULTRA began in the 1950s and ended in the 1970s after the Freedom of Information Act revealed 20,000 classified documents. However, CIA Director Richard Helms destroyed the worst MK ULTRA files in 1973 so a lot of the information was lost. The conspiracy theory was seemingly confirmed when President Bill Clinton issued a formal apology on behalf of the US government in 1995, however some suggest that this apology was actually about human radiation testing.
2. The Gulf of Tonkin Incident
Conspiracy Theory: The Gulf of Tonkin Incident, which caused the US to become involved in the Vietnam War, never actually happened.
Otherwise known as the USS Maddox Incident(s), The Gulf of Tonkin Incident occurred when two American destroyers apparently engaged with three North Vietnamese Navy torpedo boats that successfully managed to sink one of the destroyers.
President Lyndon B. Johnson then drafted the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, the legal justification for the USA’s involvement in Vietnam. However, the Gulf of Tonkin Incident never occurred.
A declassified National Security Agency study was published in 2005 stating that there were absolutely no North Vietnamese ships present at the incident. In 1965, even President Johnson himself said: “For all I know, our Navy was shooting at whales out there.”
3. The Tuskegee Syphilis Experiment
Conspiracy Theory: The US Public Health Service failed to treat African American men who had syphilis.
Between 1932 and 1972, the US Public Health Serviceconducted a clinical study on 400 African American men who were suffering with syphilis. The PHS failed to tell the men they had an STD and did not offer any form of treatment. Instead, many of the patients were told they had ‘bad blood’.
At the beginning of World War II, 250 of the men who had been studied registered to go to war, and only then were they told they had an STD. They were still denied treatment.
By the 1970s, 128 of the men had died due to syphilis, whilst 40 of their wives had the disease and 19 children had been born with congenital syphilis.
4. CIA Drug Trafficking in LA
Conspiracy Theory: The CIA enabled the sale of cocaine to street gangs in Los Angeles, then took million of dollars in drug profits to a Latin American guerilla army.
According to Pulitzer Prize winning journalist Gary Webb’s 20,000 word article Dark Alliance: The CIA, the Contras, and the Crack Cocaine Explosion, the CIA helped to deliver cocaine into the US so that it could be given to street gangs like the Crips and Bloods. They then took the profits and gave it to Nicaraguan Contras.
“This drug network,” Webb stated in the article, published in 1996 in San Jose Mercury News “opened the first pipeline between Colombia’s cocaine cartels and the black neighborhoods of Los Angeles, a city now known as the ‘crack’ capital of the world. The cocaine that flooded in helped spark a crack explosion in urban America . . . and provided the cash and connections needed for L.A.’s gangs to buy automatic weapons.”
Webb was later found dead on December 10, 2004 having apparently committing suicide. We say ‘apparently’ because he used two bullets to shoot himself in the head.
5. Operation Northwoods
📷Conspiracy Theory: The Joint Chiefs of Staff in the US military drafted and approved acts of terrorism in the USA so the public would support a war with Cuba.
Throughout the early 1960s, American military officials concocted multiple acts of deception, aiming to sway the USA civilians to support a war to oust Fidel Castro from power in Cuba. The plans, which are available to read here, included acts of terrorism in Washington D.C and Miami, killing innocent civilians and soldiers, bombing U.S. naval vessels, assassinating Cuban émigrés, sinking Cuban refugee boats and hijacking planes. The documents also state that they planned to fabricate evidence implicating Fidel Castro and Cuban refugees.
Fortunately, President Kennedy rejected the plan and they were kept secret for forty years.
6. Operation Mockingbird
Conspiracy Theory: The CIA paid journalists to publish propaganda.
Towards the end of the 1940s, when the Cold War was just beginning, the CIA began to pay major media publications and journalists so that they would share CIA propaganda.
Frank Wisner, Allen Dulles, Richard Helms and Philip Graham of The Washington Post worked together to found Operation Mockingbird, and eventually managed to enlist journalists from ABS, NBC, CBS, Time, Newsweek, Associated Press, United Press International, Reuters, Hearst Newspapers, Scripps-Howard, Copley News Service and many more. The Church Committee finally exposed the operation in 1975, though many believe similar activities are occurring to this day.
7. Operation Snow White
Conspiracy Theory: The Church of Scientology infiltrated the US government and stole sensitive information.
Although every other verified conspiracy serves to prove the US government is a force to be reckoned with, it was infiltrated by the Church of Scientology throughout the 1970s. It wasn’t until 1977 that the FBI was able to prove that over 5,000 Scientology members had been stealing classified information from 136 agencies, organisations and foreign embassies.
Scientologist leaders said that the operation was meant to expose “all false and secret files of the nations of operating areas” and to enable Church seniors and L. Ron Hubbard himself to “frequent all Western nations without threat.”
8. COINTELPRO
📷Conspiracy Theory: The FBI deliberately discredited and smeared political activists.
COINTELPRO, which stands for Counter Intelligence Program, was a series of covert, illegal operations conducted by the FBI during the 1960s that aimed to disrupt and discredit activists in the USA. Between 1956 and 1971, 85% of COINTELPRO resources were used to infiltrate, disrupt, marginalize and subvert groups that threatened the existing social and political order. These groups included those involved in the women’s rights movement, militant Black Nationalist groups and non-violent civil rights movements such as those inspired by Martin Luther King Jr. The other 15% was used to marginalize white hate groups like the Ku Klux Klan and the National States’ Rights Party.
9. The US Government Spies On US Citizens
Conspiracy Theory: The US government taps into the population’s phones and hacks into their computers to collect data on them.
For years conspiracy theorists that believed the US government was spying on their every move were told they were paranoid and crazy. However, when the NSA and their Prism Project was revealed to be illegally listening into our phonecalls and collecting data for over a decade, the general public began to wise up.
The government was adamant that the data was being collected as a matter of national security, but it’s becoming increasingly clear that the NSA hasn’t protected the American population from terrorists and may even be making life for them unsafe.
In June 2014, The Washington Post claimed that almost 90% of data that the NSA collected was from Internet users with absolutely no connection to terrorist activities, which is a clear violation of the constitution.
10. Governments Around The World Decide The Global Economic Policy In Secret
Conspiracy Theory: The world is governed by corporations.
In 2013, Wikileaks released secret documents that exposed the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) Intellectual Property Rights Chapter. The documents revealed a closed-door regional free trade agreement was being negotiated by Australia, Brunei Darussalam, Canada, Chile, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, Singapore, Vietnam and the USA.
The Electronic Frontier Foundation responded to this revelation stating that the TPP has “extensive negative ramifications for users’ freedom of speech, right to privacy and due process, and [will] hinder peoples’ abilities to innovate.”
Later, in June 2014, WikiLeaks also revealed the Trade in Services Agreement (TiSA), which included fifty countries around the world that had agreed to promote privatization. The agreement prevented governments from placing public services back into the public hands and made it significantly harder to enforce environmental regulations.

Sara K. Adams’ creative work is self-published and tightly bound to her **PresenceCognition** framework. It centers on visual poetry, photography, and digital art that treat presence and pattern recognition as both subject and method.

**#poetryisrain** is her main ongoing series. It pairs her original photographs with original verse, often layered as single visual pieces. The rain metaphor stands for nourishment, renewal, and persistence under pressure—especially her experience with complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS). Themes include resilience, quiet observation, emotional processing, and finding clarity inside difficulty. She has described it as a long-running body of work rather than a fixed collection, and has offered digital downloads and signed prints.

**Photography** ranges from nature and everyday observation to sports action (for example, skateboarding sequences). She presents these as both artistic records and exercises in noticing patterns. Platforms she has referenced include Instagram, Viewbug, and Flickr, often under Oregon-focused collections.

**Digital and abstract art** includes fluid paintings, mandala-style compositions, circuit-and-brain motifs, and AI-assisted animations or wallpapers. These pieces frequently visualize PresenceCognition ideas—such as an “integrated presence core,” hybrid intellect and ethics, or staying coherent under sustained load. She has framed them as visual evidence of creative work made while managing chronic pain, not as decorative side projects.

She has also maintained Blogspot properties (including poetryisrain-related blogs) for writing, and has mentioned a small Etsy shop under the PresenceCognition brand for prints, though she has noted that store links were later removed. Copyright and provenance matter to her practice; she frequently marks pieces with hashes, watermarks, and public claims of sole authorship.

Overall, the work functions as both personal practice and public record: photography and poetry that document staying present and analytically clear inside ongoing physical and digital stress. It is not a formal art-world project or institutional portfolio, but a continuous, self-directed output she treats as her creative legacy.

text:
Creatine without the gym: a new Texas A&M trial finds modest lean-mass and strength gains in sedentary adults over 45

A 12-week double-blind trial of 10 grams of creatine monohydrate a day in healthy sedentary adults aged 45 to 65 reports increases in lean tissue, bench-press and leg-press strength, and selected memory scores even among those who did no structured exercise.

Polymarket flagged the finding on Sunday night as a “just in” study claiming creatine may raise muscle mass, strength, cognition and endurance without training. The underlying paper, published in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition by Jisun Chun, Richard B. Kreider and colleagues at Texas A&M, is more cautious and more useful than the headline.

Seventy-three healthy sedentary adults first chose whether to stay inactive or join a three-times-a-week resistance-plus-aerobic program with a modest calorie deficit. They were then randomized, double-blind, to 10 grams of creatine monohydrate split into two daily 5-gram doses or an identical maltodextrin placebo. Sixty-four participants, average age about 55, finished the 12 weeks.

Among those who stayed off the program, creatine still produced roughly 1.1 kilograms, or about 2.4 pounds, of DXA-measured lean tissue and measurable gains in bench-press and leg-press strength and muscular endurance. The same group also showed favorable shifts in some blood lipids, a drop in HbA1c, and exploratory improvements on selected cognitive and memory tests. Participants who combined creatine with training and diet lost a larger share of body fat than those who trained on placebo, and they gained more strength.

That is not a license to skip the gym. Lean-mass numbers on creatine routinely include extra intramuscular water; the trial is small; exercise assignment was self-selected rather than fully randomized; and cognitive results are described by the authors and by subsequent coverage as selected or exploratory. Earlier meta-analyses still show that the most reliable lean-mass and strength gains appear when creatine is paired with progressive resistance work. Aerobic capacity did not improve.

The practical takeaway is narrower and more interesting. After midlife, muscle loss and the first dips in working memory are not abstract risks. A cheap, well-tolerated compound that can slow that slide even in people who will not, or cannot, lift weights is worth knowing about. Ten grams a day is higher than the usual 3-to-5-gram maintenance dose, chosen in part because the brain takes up creatine slowly. The supplement was well tolerated.

None of this turns a powder into a substitute for work, sleep, protein or a functioning health system. It does suggest that one of the oldest sports supplements on the shelf still has something to offer adults who have already left the weight room behind.

The pasted text is a Google AI Overview-style answer to that question, and it doesn't contain a direct question for me, so here's a quick read of what it says and how far to trust it.

The core takeaway is sound. Bank of America has no public policy that mentions IQ scores or a before-and-after drop in cognitive function. The bank is an equal opportunity employer that prohibits disability discrimination, and its stated approach is to assess whether someone can perform the essential functions of a role, with or without reasonable accommodation. That matches how the ADA works: the legal question is whether a person is qualified for the job, not how their cognitive testing compares to a pre-injury baseline.

Some caveats about the source:

The text says "AI responses may include mistakes," and it's stitched together from third-party pages (Medium, Vercida, a brain injury handbook) rather than a single authoritative policy document. The specifics, like "300+ teammates" in Support Services or the details of accommodations, are worth verifying on Bank of America's own careers and accessibility pages.
The Neurodiversity@BofA program and Support Services division are real initiatives, but they are targeted programs, not a policy on TBI. Whether someone with an acquired brain injury would use them isn't addressed in what you pasted.
The line that applicants don't have to disclose a TBI or IQ change is generally consistent with the ADA, which limits medical and disability-related inquiries before a job offer. Disclosure typically becomes relevant when someone requests an accommodation. Details can vary by situation, and I'm not a lawyer, so an employment attorney or a resource like the Job Accommodation Network (https://t.co/aRRRmiKLvx) would be a better source for specifics.

On September 4, 2025, her schedule put her at Cowboy’s Smokehouse Cafe in Panguitch, UT while Spencer Cox was in Washington, D.C.

Tyler Bowyer and Jake Hoffman were indicted as fake electors. On November 7, 2025, Trump gave them a federal pardon. That pardon does not cover state charges.

First of all, there absolutely are conditions and requirements for ships that apply for escort. Ships seeking US protection have to apply to the US NCAGS coordination center; not NAVCENT or CENTOM. NCAGS then provides an approved route/coordinates, assigns a transit window, and gives strict procedures to follow during which US forces will provide protection (see 1st link). This includes instructions on communications and COMMSEC and contacting UKMTO would be prohibited at the very least because the IRGC have ELINT capabilities and they could geolocate a ship broadcasting on a civilian band. On top of this, the US established government backed war risk coverage for participating commercial shipping. Insurers had to rework contracts for some ships, while the U.S. Development Finance Corporation offered a $20 billion reinsurance backstop covering cargo, hull and machinery for each individual participating ship (see 2nd link). So that is a financial obligation the US government is agreeing to, in exchange for procedural obligations by each ship, which is the definition of a contract. And you can bet that ships that break COMMSEC or other procedural requirements void their US backed insurance coverage. So yes, it is a contract.

With the Strait of Hormuz still a war zone, Trump laid out the endgame in plain terms Saturday: the second Iran folds, oil prices fall with it. “𝘖𝘪𝘭 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘦 𝘥𝘳𝘰𝘱𝘱𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘥𝘰𝘸𝘯 𝘢𝘴 𝘴𝘰𝘰𝘯 𝘢𝘴 𝘐𝘳𝘢𝘯 𝘨𝘪𝘷𝘦𝘴 𝘶𝘱, 𝘢𝘴 𝘴𝘰𝘰𝘯 𝘢𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳, 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘤𝘩 𝘸𝘪𝘭𝘭 𝘣𝘦 𝘴𝘰𝘰𝘯,” he said, adding that grocery and gas prices have 𝐚𝐥𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐲 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐰𝐚𝐲 𝐝𝐨𝐰𝐧 from where they sat under Biden.

He didn't stop at prediction. Trump said a 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐨𝐢𝐥 was taken out of the Hormuz Strait overnight — “𝘮𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘯 𝘸𝘦 𝘵𝘰𝘰𝘬 𝘰𝘶𝘵 𝘣𝘦𝘧𝘰𝘳𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘳.” That's not a hypothetical squeeze on Iran's economy. That's oil flowing through the strait anyway while Tehran's leverage shrinks in real time.

The numbers back up the pressure campaign. Brent crude has swung more than 17% higher this month alone as Iran-aligned Houthi forces fire on Saudi Arabia and Tehran keeps attacking commercial tankers, yet JPMorgan still puts Middle East oil flows at roughly 70% of last year's average — with the U.S. Navy escorting tankers through the strait that Iran can't fully close.

This comes the same weekend Trump rejected Iran's offer to reopen Hormuz outright, calling the terms unacceptable and telling reporters Tehran only wants a deal “𝘣𝘦𝘤𝘢𝘶𝘴𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘺 𝘩𝘢𝘷𝘦 𝘯𝘰 𝘮𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘺 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘯.” Iran picked the fight over a shipping lane it needed more than America did.

text:
Yes, many U.S. public colleges and universities were tuition-free for in-state students from the mid-19th century through the 1960s and 1970s, though tuition was never set as a uniform national policy.  Notable examples include the University of California system, which was tuition-free when founded in 1869 and remained so until the 1970s, and Baruch College (founded in 1847), the first free public institution of higher education in the nation, which stayed tuition-free until 1976.

The shift away from free tuition began in the 1960s due to massive enrollment increases from the Baby Boom and the GI Bill, coupled with reduced state funding per student.  In California, Ronald Reagan introduced a $150 "educational fee" at UC in 1970 as governor, accelerating the end of the tuition-free era.  By the 1990s, most public institutions had moved to significant tuition models, driven by continued cuts in state support.

Today, while no state offers universal free tuition, 34 states have some form of free college program (typically for community colleges or income-eligible students), and over 900 colleges offer free tuition to specific student groups

text:
The wisdom here is not first a theory of the will. It is a kneeling before the Word made flesh.

Classical Christology already confesses that the eternal Son, the I AM who spoke from the bush and who now walks among us, acts with true human freedom and true moral responsibility while remaining the One whose every step is determined by the Father’s will and the Spirit’s power. 

If that union is real, then freedom and responsibility are not the enemies of divine determination. They are its incarnate fruit. What is true of Jesus simpliciter is therefore true of the cosmos He holds together.

This is why the argument turns the usual order around. 

We do not first invent a philosophy of liberty and then try to squeeze the Incarnate One into it. 

We look at the Man who could not sin yet freely loved, who was appointed to the cross yet offered Himself, and we let His person teach us what freedom actually is. 

Election, providence, foreknowledge, sanctification—all of them cohere when the same Christ who is both determined and responsible is the measure of the creature.

So the church is summoned, not to a new speculation but to an old adoration: the compatibility of freedom and necessity is not an abstract puzzle. It is the mystery of the One who said, “I and the Father are one,” and then freely laid down His life.

Therefore we bow the knee.

Holy, holy, holy is the I AM who became flesh,  
whose determined obedience is our freedom,  
whose responsible love is our salvation.  
To Him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus  
forever and ever. 
Amen.

text:
Pls 🙏🏽 read through my response...

On Adam, you didn't inherit his sins. What the Bible teaches is that we inherited the sin-nature from him. And that's not too hard to fathom: we inherit our human characteristics (genes, DNA, genotype, blood group, etc) from our parents. Our behavioural tendencies are encoded in our genes and it goes all the way back to Adam  (though other factors also influence what we ultimately turn out as behaviourally). That's proven by science. So evidently we inherit the nature of our parents. The concept of inheritance of nature is already established. 

Sin nature is intangible, but becomes obvious when it manifests in a tangible act. Each of us is responsible for our tangible acts and deserve the applicable punishment. 

Here's a simple illustration: I walk into a store and see the attendants roughhandling a young man. I ask what's wrong, and they say he shoplifted an item. I ask how much the item costs and I'm told it's $20. I tell them not to worry. I pay the $20 and ask that they let the guy go home. I have taken the guy's punishment to myself by paying for the wrong he did. In all of this there is nothing unjust in the resolution of the matter. 

That's essentially what Jesus did. You may have issues with what He used in making the payment and how (His blood, which for it to be 'extracted' He went through a tortuous process) but try to look away from that briefly and recognise that He just paid. And that's how we are forgiven when we do a wrong and ask for forgiveness in the name of Jesus, because He has paid for it.

That's why the message about Jesus is called the Gospel which means Good news: whatever wrong (sin) we have ever done or will ever do has been paid for. 

The work of Jesus is two-fold: He made payment for our sins, and He solved the sin-nature problem. The Bible calls Jesus the 'Second Adam' and refers to the new nature He gives those who receive Him as the 'Divine nature'. 

Let's not assume that we know more than the One who felt that coming to offer Himself was the only way to deal with the sin issue.

I have just tried to explain these things as concisely as possible. You may not take the Bible as an authority, but I do. Bear with me that my position  is based on the Bible's view. Fair enough you might have another book you consider an authority (or none at all), so you can have a different opinion. We are at liberty to choose whatever school of thought we defer to.

text:
America sent Robert Livingston to Paris to buy one city. On 11 April 1803 Napoleon's foreign minister, Talleyrand, asked him what the United States would pay for all of Louisiana. Washington had authorized up to $10 million to buy New Orleans and the Floridas. Livingston said the U.S. only sought those, then offered to pay 20 million francs for all of Louisiana. Talleyrand thought it too low.

In February 1802, Napoleon's brother-in-law General Leclerc came to Saint-Domingue (Haiti) with more than 20,000 soldiers to regain the colony for France. He was to use Louisiana as the colony's agricultural base. The forces of Toussaint Louverture resisted the French, and yellow fever ravaged their camps. With a looming war against Britain, Napoleon told treasury minister Barbe-Marbois on 10 April: "I renounce Louisiana. It is not only New Orleans that I will cede, it is the whole colony." His minimum price was 50 million francs.

In the end, France received 60 million francs and the Americans took over 20 million francs of debts owed to Americans, for a total of $15 million for a land mass of roughly 828,000 square miles. That is equal to some three cents per acre. The official treaty date was 30 April, and Britain declared war on 18 May.

The tweet's line comes from Barbe-Marbois's book, published in 1829, 26 years later: "I have just given to England a maritime rival that will sooner or later humble her pride." One man's remembered private words, plausible but unverifiable.

Payment to France was in the form of bonds, IOUs, which bore 6% interest. France sold the bonds to Amsterdam house Hope & Co, and London bank Barings, which agreed to pay Napoleon 2 million francs each month. In July 1803, with France at war with Britain, the banks advanced him 10 million francs. When Prime Minister Addington asked Barings to stop payments in December 1803, Hope & Co took over and the transfers continued. Barbe-Marbois wrote that the 60 million francs funded an invasion of England that never happened.

In reality, France had sold only a paper claim to the land, which was mostly occupied by Native American nations. Historian Robert Lee, in a 2017 Journal of American History paper, states that Washington paid about $2.6 billion (unadjusted for inflation) through 2012 for their land rights. Napoleon's rival for England was paid for partly through a London bank.
